sum: ServiceNow outlined a sharper shift toward agentic artificial intelligence, autonomous workers and consumption-based revenue at the BMO Capital Technology and Innovation Leaders Conference on Thursday, November 12. Investing.com reported that management described strong demand in employee and business workflows but also pointed to intensifying competition.

ServiceNow said agentic use increased 13 times year over year, while AI Control Tower adoption rose six times. More than half of third-quarter revenue came from non-seat-based models, highlighting the growing role of usage and outcomes alongside traditional seat licensing.

EmployeeWorks generated 100 million US dollars in revenue during the first three quarters of the fiscal year. The unit closed 10 deals worth more than 1 million US dollars in the third quarter, while customer count rose 60 percent during the quarter.

The company is targeting spending pools beyond traditional software and information technology budgets, including business-process outsourcing. Management said autonomous workers can handle service requests, invoice processing, collections and procurement tasks, with enterprise governance and workflow orchestration positioned as differentiators.

Executives also said seats were still growing and expected to continue growing in calendar year 2027. At the same time, smaller specialists are becoming more credible competitors, particularly in finance and procurement, increasing the pressure on ServiceNow to demonstrate customer value and effective controls.

ServiceNow stock traded at 90.97 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 16:42 CET on Friday, November 13. That was 1.99 percent below the 92.82-euro Lang & Schwarz quote in our November 6 coverage; the multi-day move is separate from a single-session market comparison.

ServiceNow (NOW) is 42% below its December high, and analysts have cut their average target by a third over the past year. Piper Sandler still sees $175.

The slide began in mid-December and deepened this year as investors worried that AI agents would replace the human users ServiceNow charges for. The stock bottomed at $83 in April. ServiceNow Puts Customer Wins Ahead of AI Rhetoric as Guidance Rises and Headcount Falls
sum: ServiceNow is asking investors to judge its artificial intelligence push by what happens on customers' desks rather than on its own slide decks. The company's latest disclosures — a measurable productivity gain at Keysight Technologies, an expanded role at the NBA, a deeper tie-up with OpenAI and a raised subscription forecast — all point the same way, provided the anecdotes eventually show up in signed contracts.

The stakes are higher because the wider sector has turned jittery. According to Associated Press, technology and AI shares came under pressure on Thursday amid worries about valuations and spending. Reuters reported roughly two weeks ago that disappointing results from ServiceNow and Fortinet weighed on software stocks and sharpened concerns about AI-driven disruption. Skepticism, in other words, is not confined to one vendor.

The most tangible evidence arrived on Thursday, when ServiceNow said Keysight Technologies uses its customer management software with CPQ to configure and generate quotes. Keysight reported that sales staff produced quotes 40% faster, while the time spent setting up and maintaining configurations fell by 50–80%.

Those are hard numbers tied to a specific workflow: getting to a quote sooner and spending less time on its technical groundwork. For investors, such figures carry more weight than broad AI claims, as long as customers can confirm the improvements in day-to-day operation. The economic argument only gains force, however, when clients expand their usage or book additional services.

A second reference case came on Wednesday, when ServiceNow extended its partnership with the NBA. The league is to deploy ServiceNow EmployeeWorks for onboarding new staff and handling internal workplace requests. Here the emphasis is on intended use; the product choice speaks for ServiceNow only if the expected benefit holds up in practice.

The partnership expansion announced on October 28 fits the same pattern. It covers a ServiceNow plugin for ChatGPT and the use of ServiceNow in OpenAI's own operations, alongside planned integrations for cybersecurity and the development of AI-powered agents.

sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Shares of ServiceNow (NOW) have lost 40.6% over the past year, while the S&P 500 returned 11.9%. The sharpest single-day decline occurred on October 29, 2026, when the shares fell 27%. To determine whether the selling is nearly done, investors can start with what is known: at $109.16, the stock has returned to a price it has reached several times since 2023. So has this price held for ServiceNow stock before?

It has held three times since 2023, though not on every visit. The first two tests began just six weeks apart, meaning their subsequent gains overlap. On August 9, 2023, the stock closed at $110.07, and its highest close within a year was 50.6% above that level. Buyers returned on September 22, 2023, at $110.82. That rally extended further, achieving a peak close 69.2% above its starting point within a year.

The latest bounce materialized this summer. Shares closed at $110.07 on July 30, 2026, and advanced to $138.43 by August 27. That same level failed to hold earlier in 2026, however. Following visits in February, March and June, the stock declined 5% before it could manage a 20% rally.

A $10,000 investment in ServiceNow at today's price would grow to about $12,450 at resistance of $135.86, a level where a previous rally stalled once before. Along the way, the stock would encounter another threshold at $124.34, where a different rally also stalled once. The advance that began from this price this summer broke through both levels, eventually reaching a peak close of $158.96. Matching the typical bounce from this level in 2023 would turn the same $10,000 into $15,990. A move to resistance is therefore smaller than the stock's historical bounces from this price.

The business behind any potential bounce is growing slightly below its historical pace. ServiceNow's revenue rose 21.8% over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, arriving a touch under its three-year average of 22.1%. The company's operating margin over those twelve months fell to 9.7%, down from 13.9% a year earlier.

ServiceNow’s Raised Guidance Is Not the Issue — the Market Is Arguing With the Forward Curve
sum: ServiceNow’s latest quarterly report contained two stories, and the market only wanted to hear one of them. Subscription revenue climbed 21% to $3,988 million in the third quarter of 2026 — a figure that describes a business still expanding at a healthy clip. Yet the shares suffered their largest single-day loss in company history on Thursday, then shed another 3.2% on Friday as the wider software sector stayed under pressure.

The gap between those two facts is where the real analysis begins. Thursday’s selloff, as reported by Reuters, was tied to earnings that fell short of expectations and to a softer growth outlook for cRPO — the current remaining performance obligation that functions as a forward-looking gauge of booked business. A broad industry retreat, disappointing results from Fortinet, and fresh worries about artificial intelligence displacing established software vendors added fuel. Company-specific disappointments and sector-wide anxiety arrived at the same time, which makes it easy to misread one for the other.

Current remaining performance obligation grew 20.5% in the quarter. For the closing quarter of the year, management guided to 18.5%. That deceleration — modest on paper — is the detail that reframed the entire report for investors. A company can post robust growth and still miss the market’s test, because what gets priced is not the quarter just delivered but the trajectory implied for the one ahead.

Against that, ServiceNow raised its full-year 2026 subscription revenue outlook to a range of $15,780 million to $15,790 million. It also lifted its target for annual AI contract value in 2026 to $1.7 billion, and on Wednesday pushed up its projected adjusted free cash flow margin for the full year to 36%. Those are not the numbers of a business in retreat. They are, however, promises rather than results — and the distinction matters enormously when sentiment has already turned.

The bull case does not rest on cost discipline alone. ServiceNow is simultaneously holding out higher revenue and a richer cash conversion rate. What would make that combination genuinely persuasive is evidence that both targets hold together.

sum: ServiceNow shares shed 3.2% on Friday, extending a slide that began after the company's quarterly report and carried the wider software sector down with it. The headline number tells you the stock fell. It doesn't tell you why — and the gap between those two things is where the actual investment case sits.

The selloff had two ingredients. Reuters reported Thursday that software names came under pressure following disappointing results from both ServiceNow and Fortinet, with fears about AI-driven disruption weighing on sentiment across the sector. For ServiceNow specifically, company-specific growth expectations collided with a weak industry backdrop. The crucial distinction: the displacement worry is an investor concern, not a documented business loss.
The third quarter of 2026 produced $4.106 billion in revenue, up 20.5% year over year. Subscription revenue reached $3.988 billion, a 21% increase. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.00.

Those figures describe a business that is still expanding at a healthy clip. They do not, however, answer the question investors were asking — namely, how fast growth will proceed from here. And that is precisely where the market's objection lay.

ServiceNow guided to 18.5% cRPO growth for the fourth quarter, a forecast Reuters noted fell short of consensus. The company also raised its full-year subscription revenue outlook and lifted its 2026 AI annual contract value target to $1.7 billion. It separately increased its free cash flow margin guidance for the year to 36%.

So the picture is not one of deterioration. It is one of expectations that ran ahead of guidance. Higher corporate targets on one side, a more cautious read on near-term growth quality on the other. An elevated AI contract target doesn't by itself refute displacement fears — and those fears, in turn, don't prove operational weakness.

Against that ambiguous backdrop, two customer decisions announced Wednesday deserve more attention than they typically get. Hewlett Packard Enterprise selected ServiceNow to overhaul customer support and field operations in its cloud and AI business. That is a concrete commitment from a named enterprise, not another product launch.

sum: The subscription business model now dominates much of the software industry and that has fueled the rise of software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks. SaaS companies sell cloud-based software through subscriptions, delivering regular updates to customers and recurring revenue to the business.

That steady revenue has fueled strong investor interest. Many SaaS stocks still trade at premium valuations, a trend that accelerated during the pandemic, though AI start-ups like Anthropic have pressured valuations more recently. Paying too much can limit long-term returns, but not every SaaS company is priced for perfection. A handful offer more reasonable valuations alongside solid growth potential.
If you want to invest in SaaS companies that are reasonably valued, these seven options, Microsoft, Adobe, Salesforce, Shopify, Palantir, ServiceNow, and CrowdStrike, are a good place to start.

For 45 years, Microsoft (MSFT +6.58%) has dominated the market for traditional software. Microsoft Windows is the standard operating system for PCs, and Microsoft Office remains the productivity suite of choice for enterprises around the world.

However, Microsoft's dominance was tested by the proliferation of mobile devices that do not use Windows, as well as competition from Alphabet's (GOOG +3.90%) (GOOGL +3.82%) Google products, including Google Workspace, Docs, Sheets, and Slides.

Microsoft eventually abandoned its PC-centric strategy, bringing first-rate versions of its Office applications to Apple products and mobile devices, and launching Office 365, now Microsoft 365, a subscription-based version of Office. With Microsoft 365 garnering at least 89 million consumer subscribers and more than 450 million paid commercial seats, Microsoft has preserved its lead in the productivity software market.

Microsoft isn't a pure-play SaaS company, and its stock has historically been expensive relative to earnings. But the company has successfully transitioned to selling subscription-based software and grown its SaaS business by double digits while maintaining its market dominance. Both revenue and earnings have been growing swiftly, driven by its success in SaaS and the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI).

The catalyst belonged to someone else: Salesforce posted a blowout quarter Wednesday night, and the read-through rippled into every enterprise-software name investors had spent the spring punishing.

A stock that moves double digits on a competitor’s print is priced by sentiment about a category, not by its own results. ServiceNow is still down roughly 30% from a year ago and sits well below the $194.73 it touched over the past 52 weeks. Salesforce reported revenue of $11.35 billion, up 11% year over year, raised its full-year outlook, and unveiled “Claudeforce,” a partnership embedding Anthropic’s Claude across its products. Its Agentforce AI business crossed $1.5 billion in annual recurring revenue, up 240% year over year. Enterprise software stocks sold off hard earlier this year on the fear that autonomous AI agents would hollow out demand for traditional platforms. Salesforce’s quarter offered the first hard counter-evidence that AI is adding to software spend rather than cannibalizing it. When that fear reverses, the names hit hardest bounce hardest, and few large-caps were hit harder than ServiceNow. It also got smaller tailwinds of its own: an expanded Tech Mahindra partnership announced August 20, and analyst target hikes from Bank of America to $150 and Wells Fargo to $175.

ServiceNow (NOW) has seen its stock crater 51% from recent highs, while Palantir Technologies (PLTR) has shed 18% over the past twelve months. With valuations reset, the question for investors is no longer just about growth, but about which business model proves resilient when AI itself becomes the competitor.

ServiceNow just delivered a powerful counterargument. On July 22, the company reported second-quarter results that beat the high end of its own guidance on every topline and profitability metric. Total revenues reached $3.987 billion, up 24% year over year, edging past the Wall Street consensus of roughly $3.9 billion. The closely watched current remaining performance obligations, or cRPO—contracts that will convert to revenue within twelve months—climbed 21% to $13.20 billion, or 21.5% in constant currency. More tellingly, ServiceNow closed 123 transactions carrying more than $1 million in net new annual contract value each, a jump of nearly 40% from the prior-year quarter.

sum: Artificial intelligence (AI) is evolving, and the next big trend in the technology is agentic AI -- software that can be given somewhat complex tasks to perform and then handle them independently with little to no additional human oversight. There should be a number of winners across this trend, including within the chip, cloud computing, and software spaces.
I believe these three companies will be among the biggest beneficiaries in each of these areas.

While AI model training requires the parallel processing muscle of large numbers of powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), agentic AI needs more central processing units (CPUs), which are designed for sequential processing. As Intel CFO David Zinsner recently explained, because of that shift in usage toward agentic AI, the ratio of GPUs to CPUs in data centers, which not long ago was 8 to 1, and is currently 4 to 1, is headed toward 1 to 1.

That's a huge opportunity, and one of the companies best positioned to take advantage of it is Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +11.04%), which has consistently taken market share in the server CPU space. AMD has pegged this as a $120 billion opportunity in the next few years, while Nvidia's CEO recently called it a $200 billion opportunity.

AMD is already starting to produce CPUs designed specifically for agentic AI with its new Venice CPUs manufactured using Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's latest 2-nanometer technology. These new chips feature massive memory bandwidth and have 256 cores, which act like isolated work zones. This lets the chip juggle hundreds of AI tasks at the same time. These are top-tier chips that will command premium prices and position the chip company to remain a leader in the space.

In the cloud computing infrastructure space, Amazon (AMZN -0.35%) is one of the companies best positioned for the rise of agentic AI. It has leaned into the trend through a massive partnership with OpenAI designed specifically around AI agents. The two companies have built a stateful runtime environment powered by OpenAI models that will let developers create AI agents that can remember context, access compute, and work with software tools. This environment is optimized to be run on AWS infrastructure and is integrated into its Bedrock Agentcore platform.

For example, hyperscalers are investing in cloud-based services, where clients can use generative AI for coding and to create applications instead of forking over monthly payments for many different subscription services.
While it remains to be seen whether AI will wipe out SaaS companies' businesses, the market is already taking this into account. Does that create an opportunity?

ServiceNow calls itself the "control tower" of a company, and more than 8,000 clients rely on its software to run their businesses more efficiently. This business is not going to disappear so fast. On top of that, the company is pivoting to use AI to its advantage and offer a better product. It's not unlike the fears about Alphabet losing ground to ChatGPT and other large-language models (LLMs), while the company has also used AI to its advantage.

sum: ServiceNow CEO Bill McDermott has been on a mission to persuade investors to stop thinking of his enterprise software company as a standard SaaS (software-as-a-service) business.

So far, McDermott has met with skepticism from the Street, which has been fixated on the lofty valuation of ServiceNow’s shares. The stock trades at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio that is more than twice that of some competitors, such as Salesforce. As a result, ServiceNow’s stock has declined 40% over the past year despite consistently strong results.
But on Wednesday, McDermott got yet more ammunition to wield against ServiceNow’s doubters.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings that handily beat Wall Street’s top-line and bottom-line growth forecasts for a ninth consecutive quarter. Subscription revenue for the three months ended Dec. 31 was $3.47 billion—up 21% year over year—and non-GAAP earnings per share were $0.92. Both figures topped consensus estimates of roughly $3.42 billion and $0.87, respectively.

The company also raised its full-year 2026 guidance for subscription revenue, forecasting it will make between $15.53 billion to $15.57 billion. This implies growth of roughly 20% to 21%—well above the 18% to 18.5% that analysts had expected.

sum: Cloud software stocks have started this year where they left off in 2025: sell-off mode.
The continued downward spiral is setting the stage for a flurry of acquisitions, investors told CNBC.

The WisdomTree Cloud Computing Fund, which tracks cloud software, has dropped more than 8% so far this year, while the Nasdaq is slightly up. Leading software names like Salesforce, ServiceNow and Adobe are down more than 14% after badly underperforming the market a year ago.

The overriding concern is that artificial intelligence will eventually displace key pieces of the enterprise stack, as IT buyers turn to AI agents to handle tasks currently handled by software vendors, both large and small. Those fears were amplified last week when Anthropic's Claude launched an AI agent tool named Cowork that is aimed at the enterprise customer.

A senior investor at a large private equity fund who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the subject said the disruption in software is happening today and will force several midsized software companies to seek financing options, potentially spurring acquisitions by private equity.

Orlando Bravo, co-founder of software-focused buyout firm Thoma Bravo, is looking to buy the dip, and sees value in companies that are building their own agentic solutions to work with their existing systems.

The Armis acquisition would further augment ServiceNow’s security capabilities. California-based Armis specializes in agentless cybersecurity that helps identify and track security threats on devices across industries.
